articles.title: Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works
articles.teaser: Sovereignty is the ability to move: take away each dot on the map, and keep a twin that works for the minimum viable company, tested in QA.

figures.caption: Take away the dot, in three frames. One service as it runs; object storage removed and the blast radius followed up the edges to the customers; a twin of the storage, tested in QA, putting the service back for the priority customers, degraded but running. Use the controls to stop on each frame.

A maturity model for every dot you do not control. From 0, it stops, through the data can leave, it runs somewhere once, it runs for the minimum viable company, to 4, it moves when you decide. Each level carries a cost and a population it serves, and each is only real if it was tested.

graph.teaser: Sovereignty is the ability to move: take away each dot on the map, and keep a twin that works for the minimum viable company, tested in QA.
graph.core_idea: Europe's sovereignty conversation is mostly about frontier models, data centres and GPUs, which is playing where the ball is rather than where it is going; sovereignty is the ability to move workloads and actions, which most organisations lack because everything is hard-coded and never deployed twice; the test is a Wardley map where each dot is taken away and the blast radius followed up to the customer, across the whole stack; the answer is not an alternative as good as today but a twin that works for the minimum viable company, run in QA all the time, scored on a maturity model; ask whether it can move before asking whether it is cheap; only open source gives control that survives an acquisition; Europe lacks a commercial open source model, not startups or talent; some of this should be provided centrally like a road; and models and twins now make the analysis possible at scale.

nodes.label: The conversation is about things Europe does not control
nodes.summary: Frontier models, giant data centres and GPUs take years and capital and benefit whoever already has them.

nodes.label: Play where the ball is going
nodes.summary: A good padel player has time because they read the ball and move to where it will be; moving after it comes off the glass is hopeless.

nodes.label: Sovereignty is the ability to move
nodes.summary: Agility, almost liquidity: moving workloads and actions between providers, even within one cloud, which most organisations cannot do.

nodes.label: Critical means the business stops
nodes.summary: For a company a supplier disruption that stops the service is critical whether or not it is national infrastructure.

nodes.label: Take away the dot
nodes.summary: On a Wardley map remove one thing you do not control and follow the blast radius up to the customer; if the service stops, take it to the board.

nodes.label: Every dot must be replaceable, built or bought
nodes.summary: Custom-built systems stand on commodities, and one only a single person can deploy is a single point of failure too.

nodes.label: Do not jump from zero to a hundred
nodes.summary: The alternative does not have to be as good as today; it has to work, slower and dearer if need be.

nodes.label: The minimum viable company
nodes.summary: The smallest version of the business that keeps serving the priority customers while the rest recovers; a backup of operations, not only data.

nodes.label: A twin for every dot you do not control
nodes.summary: Compatible enough that the application cannot tell, on infrastructure you can run; the S3 twin exists, the others are the work.

nodes.label: Can it move: a maturity model
nodes.summary: 0 it stops, 1 the data can leave, 2 it runs somewhere once, 3 it runs for the minimum viable company, 4 it moves when you decide.

nodes.label: Run it in QA, all the time
nodes.summary: Disposable QA environments built on the twins prove each week that the business can run without the dots you do not control.

nodes.label: Can it move, then is it cheap
nodes.summary: Possibility first with a cost and scale matrix per dot; cost effectiveness second; asking the second first ends the conversation.

nodes.label: Open source, or one acquisition away
nodes.summary: A European supplier today can be bought tomorrow; only open source and Creative Commons give control that survives a change of owner.

nodes.label: Europe lacks a commercial open source model, not startups
nodes.summary: Prosus and Dealroom: as many AI startups as the US, a third of the breakout rate; 44% of US unicorn founders born abroad.

nodes.label: Provided centrally, like a road
nodes.summary: Not every company can twin every dependency; governments, industry bodies and large buyers should provide some of it as open infrastructure.

nodes.label: Models and twins make the analysis scale
nodes.summary: Mapping, removing dots and simulating the blast radius can now be done at scale, better on twins than in spreadsheets.

quotes.text: If you do not have the software, the schema and the ability to load and move it, you do not have data mobility; you have an archive.
quotes.why: Why a backup of data is not a backup of operations.

quotes.text: Even if a supplier is European today, you are one acquisition away from losing that.
quotes.why: Why only open source gives control that survives a change of owner.

articles.title: The records ran out: a fresh agent found the shared contract in two MCP calls, and where sgit and RiskMandate fit at the edges
articles.teaser: A fresh agent found a shared contract in two MCP calls from build records; where the records stopped is exactly where evidence labels and sgit vaults fit.

figures.caption: Where the records ran out, and what fills each gap. The left two columns are Ignacio Aldama's own findings; the right two are the label each one gets in the vocabulary of evidence and barriers, and what fills it today. The status column says which of those exist, which are documented and untested here, and which are proposed.

graph.teaser: A fresh agent found a shared contract in two MCP calls from build records; where the records stopped is exactly where evidence labels and sgit vaults fit.
graph.core_idea: Ignacio Aldama's test shows build-generated dependency records give a fresh Claude Code session a system's structure in two MCP calls, enough to know what not to touch, and he names where the records stop: they describe structure not behaviour, a green build can hide tests that never ran, a demo carries a public signing secret and unfinished work, and memory holds intent without being tied to a version; each edge has a name in the vocabulary of evidence levels and barriers, and is filled by labelling every fact with how it is known, treating a skipped test as an expectation, accepting a shortcut by name and for an interval, keeping memory and records in one encrypted versioned sgit history, and letting records cross company boundaries with publish, clone and mirror.

nodes.label: Two MCP calls found the shared contract
nodes.summary: A fresh session called read_scope and read_components, saw two components share one version of the ticket entity, changed only the app; 41 tests passed, nine new.

nodes.label: Knowing what is shared tells an agent what not to touch
nodes.summary: The records gave structure, and structure was enough to keep the change inside one component.

nodes.label: Records describe structure, not behaviour
nodes.summary: The route list lived in a test fake's docs and nothing checked it against the real service.

nodes.label: Label every fact with how it is known
nodes.summary: Derived, inferred, self-reported, documented, measured, observed: the route list was documented, the restart check was observed.

nodes.label: A green build can hide tests that never ran
nodes.summary: Database tests skip when CI cannot start the database, so a pass does not show they ran.

nodes.label: A skipped test is an expectation reported as a control
nodes.summary: Only a boundary is a control; count the run from what happened and drop the evidence back to documented until the test runs.

nodes.label: Demo shortcuts stay invisible
nodes.summary: A demo account and a public signing secret are a grant wider than the mandate; concurrency, migrations and recovery are still to do.

nodes.label: Accept by name, in a direction, for an interval, or stop
nodes.summary: No deny button for a deployed system; the unfinished items become conditions in a licence to operate with owners and expiries.

nodes.label: Memory holds intent but is not tied to a version
nodes.summary: A memory note is dated; a record is part of its version but carries no intent.

nodes.label: Memory and records in one encrypted versioned history
nodes.summary: In an sgit vault the intent of version 1.4 is committed at 1.4, and encryption means the sensitive intent can be written down at all.

nodes.label: Records must cross company boundaries
nodes.summary: His goal is a record that holds where the other side is outside the agent's index.

nodes.label: Publish, clone and mirror
nodes.summary: sgit publish and clone over plain GETs, vault mirror for custody without access, append lanes for writers who cannot read; documented in 0.21.0, untested here.

nodes.label: The best decision was the agent's own judgement
nodes.summary: Nothing stopped it changing a contract two components depend on: a write row held by an expectation, which a platform could make a boundary.

quotes.text: knowing what is shared also tells an agent what not to touch.
quotes.why: Aldama's own line for why structure alone was enough in his test.

quotes.text: A skipped test is a control that did not run.
quotes.why: The green-build edge in the vocabulary of barriers.

articles.title: Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch
articles.teaser: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code; a twin lets the code not know, and the value in the twin is what signs the migration.

figures.caption: The twin layer. The application keeps calling S3, EC2 and IAM exactly as it does today; the calls land on an open source twin, which is where policy, journal, encryption, versions, cost and failure injection live; the twin decides where the bytes go, and switching the backend is a setting. The S3 twin is built; EC2 and IAM are not.

What signs a migration and what does not. Sovereignty, cost and any return that depends on a future event sit on the left; value that lands the day you switch, and gives the signer cover, sits on the right. Underneath, the rule for the project: no new features during the move.

graph.teaser: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code; a twin lets the code not know, and the value in the twin is what signs the migration.
graph.core_idea: Sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is code, so the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: its S3, EC2 and IAM calls land on an open source twin the client cannot tell from the real service, and the twin decides where the bytes go; the S3 twin exists; the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost, which are important and never urgent, but value that lands the day you switch and gives the signer cover, backups, versions, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip and cost per workload, most of it supplied by an sgit vault behind the twin; the project adds no new features because it is a villager move; and an infrastructure operator in Europe can sell it as value with the risk removed.

nodes.label: Workloads do not move because moving means changing code
nodes.summary: Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is in code that works today; the cost of change is the risk, so most organisations stay whatever the policy says.

nodes.label: AWS European Sovereign Cloud, 15 January 2026
nodes.summary: A separate cloud in Brandenburg run by EU residents with zero operational control outside the EU; the code still talks to one vendor's API, so it is sovereignty by permission.

nodes.label: The application must not know
nodes.summary: Not one line changes; the same calls land on whatever backend is chosen, and the destination is a setting.

nodes.label: A twin is measured by indistinguishability
nodes.summary: An interface to a real system used by unmodified production code; a mock is for tests and measured by fidelity; switching a twin costs an endpoint, a mock a code path.

nodes.label: The S3 twin exists, as open source
nodes.summary: An S3-compatible container that boto3 and the AWS CLI cannot tell from S3, serving from real S3, a vault, local disk or memory per environment; EC2 and IAM are not built.

nodes.label: The reason to move is never sovereignty or cost
nodes.summary: Both are important and never urgent; a return that depends on a future event does not sign, and the signer needs cover if the move goes wrong.

nodes.label: The value lives in the twin because every call passes through it
nodes.summary: Backups, versions, encryption with the key elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies, cost per workload, data where it can be traded.

nodes.label: An sgit vault behind the twin supplies most of the value
nodes.summary: Files land as ciphertext with a history and keys the customer holds; the operator stores what it cannot read.

nodes.label: The move must move a top-of-register risk
nodes.summary: A migration that lands versions, backups, encryption and a journal on day one and takes an item off the top of the register is a decision someone can sign and defend.

nodes.label: No new features during the move
nodes.summary: A villager move from explorer to town planner; adding a feature makes it a product change too, and nobody can tell which broke what.

nodes.label: Testing against twins instead of mocks
nodes.summary: The same unmodified code runs against memory, a replayed journal, injected failures and the real service; the environment becomes a setting.

nodes.label: Every piece of software should run unmodified against a twin of every dependency
nodes.summary: Software that can only run against one provider's live API cannot be tested, moved or put behind a policy.

nodes.label: A closed twin layer moves the lock-in
nodes.summary: Open source here is independence, not generosity: you can read it, run it, fix it and move it.

nodes.label: A business model for an infrastructure operator
nodes.summary: Sell the twin in front of the real service first, then the backend switch per environment; margin in the twin layer, storage priced as the commodity it is; the hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself.

nodes.label: Start with S3, in front of the real service, then policies, then switch
nodes.summary: S3 is the most used and already twinned; journal first with nothing moving; measure what policies would have stopped; then one environment at a time; then the next service.

quotes.text: Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission.
quotes.why: Why a sovereign region from the same vendor does not change the cost of leaving.

quotes.text: If switching costs an endpoint, migration becomes a configuration decision. If it costs a code path, it becomes a project, and projects get cancelled.
quotes.why: The whole case for twins in two sentences.

articles.title: Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it
articles.teaser: A small country should not race for GPUs: the opportunity is the plumbing its talent stands on, built once as open infrastructure, with small models.

figures.caption: A talented person in Portugal, Romania or Estonia selling a service to the world, as a Wardley map. The capital race on the right is a commodity; the red dots are the plumbing that is still custom built in most of Europe and that a state can move right; the green dots are where the market is still genesis and where the money should go.

The judo playbook in five moves: map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put the money where the market is still genesis, regulate what settled, then map again. Three examples underneath of a constraint, a small state and a public model doing it.

graph.teaser: A small country should not race for GPUs: the opportunity is the plumbing its talent stands on, built once as open infrastructure, with small models.
graph.core_idea: For a small country such as Portugal, Romania or Estonia the race for frontier models, GPUs and data centres is a commoditised layer only capital can win, and the opportunity is at the other end of the map: the plumbing a talented person needs to sell a service to the world, forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in every language, contracts and tax, which is still custom built in most of Europe and should be infrastructure the state builds once, open source and on open schemas because there is no sovereignty without the ability to leave; create the demand for alternatives before the failure, put the money where the market is still genesis, small models for every language and culture and agents with the least agency, regulate what settled, and treat constraints as the input, with Europe's values and its people on the journey.

nodes.label: Do not enter the capital race
nodes.summary: Frontier models, GPUs and data centres sit in commodity with a lead that cannot be bought back; for a small country it is the wrong end of the map.

nodes.label: The opportunity is the plumbing
nodes.summary: What stops a talented person selling to the world is company formation, cross-border hiring, payments, language, contracts and tax, each custom built today.

nodes.label: A talented person at the top of the map
nodes.summary: Anchor the map on a developer, designer, librarian or product team in a small country selling a service to a buyer abroad who would rather buy than build.

nodes.label: Fewer than one in ten firms sells across EU borders online
nodes.summary: Eurostat for 2021: 18.5% of EU enterprises sold online at home, 8.1% to other EU countries, 4.6% to the rest of the world.

nodes.label: Infrastructure is the state's job because it enables everyone
nodes.summary: The shop on the road did not pay for the road; the plumbing for selling services abroad is a road in the same sense, pooled money built once for all.

nodes.label: Estonia built the road
nodes.summary: E-Residency: 142,000 e-residents and 43,000 companies, over 4,200 founded in 2026 by mid-September; X-Road, open source under MIT, shared with Finland and Iceland.

nodes.label: No sovereignty without open source and open schemas
nodes.summary: Sovereignty means being able to leave; a road with a toll gate owned by one company is lock-in, not infrastructure.

nodes.label: What the state pays for belongs to the commons
nodes.summary: Software bought with taxes should be visible and runnable by the public, which is also how a local industry grows around it.

nodes.label: Create the demand before the day you need it
nodes.summary: Parallel services, local alternatives with fewer features, procurement that prefers data and service mobility, so a market exists before the single point of failure fails; the failures are under-documented, so the fragility is worse than the public cases show.

nodes.label: Smaller models, more of them
nodes.summary: Most work needs a model good enough for one job in one language with one culture; frontier models are for the frontier and are too expensive and too powerful for production.

nodes.label: Amalia, a public model as a public road
nodes.summary: Portugal's open model of 1 July 2026, built by universities with 5.5 million euros of EU funds, published with dataset and code as a base for others.

nodes.label: Agents with the least agency
nodes.summary: Use the model once to build the tool and run production as plain code under a behaviour policy; trust comes from less agency, not more.

nodes.label: Constraints are the input
nodes.summary: DeepSeek trained V3 in 2.788 million GPU hours on export-restricted H800 chips with custom communication code; the constraint produced the innovation.

nodes.label: A distributed workforce works when the infrastructure comes first
nodes.summary: Millions spent on Upwork as a CISO and CTO delivered faster and better because project management, structure and onboarding were built first; the right talent at a fair local price, and jobs that stay where people want to live.

nodes.label: The judo playbook in five moves
nodes.summary: Map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put money where the market is genesis, regulate what settled, then map again.

nodes.label: The embassy facilitates
nodes.summary: The Ambassador role in SGraph Send was written the way an embassy works: represent, build relationships, create the conditions for growth, never hard sales.

quotes.text: A road with a toll gate owned by one company is not infrastructure; it is lock-in with tarmac.
quotes.why: Why the plumbing has to be open source and on open schemas to count as sovereignty.

quotes.text: The talent, the energy and the hunger are not the constraint.
quotes.why: The plumbing is.

articles.title: Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map
articles.teaser: The best of our Wardley maps with their context, why the technique matters, one map read as a story, and a map inside a map inside a map.

figures.caption: Nine of the maps drawn on this site since September 2026. Every one is a claim about something real: a product that shipped, a plan that is published, a mistake that became a rule. The ninth is three maps deep.

Map one, from the outside. The anchor is a person who writes to the team. What they see, a reply with a name on it, is custom. What they do not see, the vaults, the sessions, Workspace and encrypted storage, is product or commodity. Rendered with Mermaid wardley-beta.

Map two, from the inside. The anchor is the person running the business. The dashed arrows are the movement the team is making: shared memory and the sgit CLI toward commodity, the behaviour policies, the graphs and the custom interfaces from genesis toward product. Everything rests on encrypted storage, which is already a commodity.
The reading meter at the end of 10 October, as a Wardley map: everything added that afternoon sits on the left, built on components that already existed on the right.

The map in three frames: the problem as most companies have it, what the service adds from what is already there, and where it goes. Agents in production on the explorer side, billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together; then the footprint, the twin, the policy and the graph; then cost as a discipline.

Which shoulders the passkey work stands on. Almost everything under it is a product or a commodity someone else matured; our piece is the door and a door per path; the one custom layer we had to add is the phone by QR, where a provider is not yet mature.

The agent's desktop moves from custom-built to product, on parts that are already products or commodities: Apple silicon Macs, the macOS virtual machine, the models, the desktop agent apps. State, keys and lock-down move with it, because the vaults, the PKI and the policies already exist as parts.

Map one: the verification as it runs. The person preparing the install needs confidence the tool is safe, which comes from a report, which rests on the tool's tests and on a team of agents. The six things that keep failing sit in a blob on the left, each rebuilt by hand inside a prompt every session. Files, hashes and git sit at the far right, unused.

Map two: the same verification with each piece of process made small and drawn moving right. The tool's tests and the judgment in the report stay custom, because that is the work. Everything else becomes boring on purpose, leaning on files, hashes and git.
The afternoon as a Wardley map, one release at a time: what already existed, then each feature as it was added and what it was built on, ending with what comes next. Times are UTC, from the commits.

Three altitudes of one business. The vault is a dot on the business map; zoom in and it is the anchor of the vault map, at the same place on the evolution axis; the door is a dot on that map; zoom in and it is the anchor of the door map. Up from the top is the market the business sits in, down from the bottom is a key derivation, and the axes and the reading do not change.

graph.teaser: The best of our Wardley maps with their context, why the technique matters, one map read as a story, and a map inside a map inside a map.
graph.core_idea: A Wardley map is a graph with context in two directions, a value chain anchored on a user and an evolution axis that is a choice rather than a fixed scale; read well it says what is moving the needle, whether you are optimising at the wrong altitude, what to build and what to buy, and whether a market exists, where a commoditised layer is a hard sell and custom building on top of one is the market, which answers differently for sgit and for RiskMandate; a map is a story to be read out frame by frame; every node is a map of its own, with the dot's place on the parent as the child's anchor; and the maps on this site are now published as data in each article's graph.

nodes.label: A map is a graph with two kinds of context
nodes.summary: Vertical: a value chain anchored on a person and a need, down to its dependencies. Horizontal: evolution, how mature each piece is.

nodes.label: The evolution axis is a choice
nodes.summary: Genesis to commodity is one scale; risk, data and governance can each be the axis. The map places things against a scale chosen for the question.

nodes.label: Every dot is a claim about something real
nodes.summary: A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram; positions are judgements and the judgements are the argument.

nodes.label: Optimising at the wrong altitude
nodes.summary: Polishing a component three layers below the need while the layer the user touches has not changed; the vertical axis makes it visible.

nodes.label: Build or buy, settled by the column
nodes.summary: Product or commodity: buy or vendor. Genesis or custom built on the path to the user: build.

nodes.label: Does the market exist
nodes.summary: A commoditised layer is a hard sell; a layer where everyone is custom building on top of commodities is a market.

nodes.label: sgit: the market is above the commodities
nodes.summary: Storage, version control and encryption are commodities and hard to sell; the vault is the custom layer everyone was building on top, and the product lets customers keep building above it.

nodes.label: RiskMandate: the layer below moved
nodes.summary: Agents became a commodity in the last year, so the opportunity moved up to agent behaviour, which is all genesis and custom built.

nodes.label: What is moving the needle, and where the flow leaks
nodes.summary: Which components moved and whether anything above them noticed; the attrition points are the slow, immature or borrowed dependencies, and where to hook is the mature component the custom piece can stand on.

nodes.label: A common language, and many maps
nodes.summary: Two people with a map argue about positions, without one they argue about words; the same business is mapped from different angles and altitudes, and none of them is the map.

nodes.label: The peace of a placed thing
nodes.summary: Once a thing is on a map, placed and connected, it leaves the head; most anxiety turns out to be about things far from the user.

nodes.label: A map is a story to read out, frame by frame
nodes.summary: Where is the user, what is new, what does it stand on, where did the movement happen, where did we walk back, where would somebody else hook in, what is next; the afternoon map read in eight frames.

nodes.label: A map inside a map inside a map
nodes.summary: Every node is a map, as every node of a fractal semantic graph is a graph; the dot's place on the parent's evolution axis is the child's anchor; three altitudes of this business drawn as one figure.

nodes.label: The maps published as data, as decks, and with controls
nodes.summary: Every figure now sits in its article's graph with file, URL, caption, kind and frames, so every Wardley map on the site is one query; two decks print to PDF in the browser; multi-frame maps have play, pause and step.

nodes.label: Why Wardley Maps changed how I think, 2022
nodes.summary: An Open Security Summit talk of 14 July 2022 with eleven shifts in how a problem is seen; the alternative-axis post was not found.

nodes.label: An invitation to the mapping community
nodes.summary: The maps are source, the axis-as-choice argument, and the nested reading: which of these is already known, and which is wrong.

quotes.text: A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram.
quotes.why: The reason the maps are useful in an argument: every placement is a claim that can be disagreed with.

quotes.text: Every node on a map is a Wardley map.
quotes.why: The nested reading: the dot on the parent is the anchor of the child, at the same place on the evolution axis.

articles.title: Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps
articles.teaser: Where to focus when agents can go in every direction: the place of highest leverage, shown on three days of real steps, two walked back and one parked.

figures.caption: Five choices at every step; the path only looks obvious backwards. The steps the newsroom actually took from 10 to 12 October, with the choices passed over at each, two walked back, one branch parked, and every step shipped and used before the next was chosen.

The same thing as a shape rather than a record: three to five routes open at every step, one taken and shipped, two walked a little way and walked back, one parked, and the straight line that only exists in hindsight.

Which shoulders the passkey work stands on. Almost everything under it is a product or a commodity someone else matured; our piece is the door and a door per path; the one custom layer we had to add is the phone by QR, where a provider is not yet mature.

graph.teaser: Where to focus when agents can go in every direction: the place of highest leverage, shown on three days of real steps, two walked back and one parked.
graph.core_idea: When agents can build in any direction the scarce thing is direction, and the rule is to work at the place of highest leverage, where the most value can be added now, nothing blocks, and you can start without knowing how the whole problem ends because each shipped step produces better tooling and a better view; the last three days show it, a meter to pay by depth to personas to sharing to a persona link to a reading list to a passkey design walked back and forward by a lab to real vaults and a vault pane, each shipped and used before the next was chosen, with a branch parked as valuable only with many readers; on a Wardley map the passkey work became a product in a day because its shoulders are mature commodities and the one custom layer sits where a provider is not; walking back and parking are not failures; constraints, saying no and shipping to a user who can be me; and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

nodes.label: Direction is the scarce thing
nodes.summary: Agents can build in any direction; what to build next and when to stop is the job.

nodes.label: Places of highest leverage
nodes.summary: Where the most value can be added right now, nothing blocks, and you can start; a rule about where to stand, not what to build.

nodes.label: Start without knowing how it ends
nodes.summary: By the time you reach the hard part you have better tooling and a better view; the first step's job is to produce the second step's information.

nodes.label: Guess, measure, narrow
nodes.summary: Fermi estimates, Bayesian updating, Monte Carlo ranges: the first number is not the point, the range after a few steps is.

nodes.label: Constraints and saying no
nodes.summary: Tokens, hours, attention and focus are why it works; FIRE and knowing when to stop; saying no is most of the work with agents.

nodes.label: Three days, step by step
nodes.summary: Meter, pay by depth, personas, encrypted share, persona link, reading list, passkey design, the lab's correction, real vaults, the vault pane; each shipped and used before the next.

nodes.label: Walking back is a two-way door
nodes.summary: The door removed, then put back by a test, in twelve hours; cheap because the design was shipped as something you could press.

nodes.label: Parking is not failure
nodes.summary: The wire's scheduling parked with a dated reason, valuable only with many readers; the feedback loop on what exists is the leverage today.

nodes.label: The path only looks obvious backwards
nodes.summary: Five choices at every step forwards; the discipline that replaces foresight is shipping and using each step before choosing the next.

nodes.label: Which shoulders, on the map
nodes.summary: The passkey work became a product in a day because its stack is mature commodities; the custom layer sits where a provider, the QR path, is not.

nodes.label: Shipped, and used, even by me
nodes.summary: Nothing stays a hypothesis; a step that was used tells you where the next one is.

nodes.label: The brief depends on the possible
nodes.summary: The inbox brief could not be written until the vault ran; the art of the possible is what shipping leaves behind.

articles.title: Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering
articles.teaser: A business plan: read the logs a company already has, draw each agent's footprint, twin and policy, and find the money first and the engineering second.

figures.caption: The map in three frames: the problem as most companies have it, what the service adds from what is already there, and where it goes. Agents in production on the explorer side, billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together; then the footprint, the twin, the policy and the graph; then cost as a discipline.

The problem. The person who pays the bill sees a total. Below it, agents in production built from prompts and workflows grown in sessions, on commodity model APIs metered by the token, with logs, traces and invoices that exist and are never read together, and no one who owns the cost.
Observe, map, find: the three steps, the two lists, how it makes money, why vaults, and the positive frame. Every price is a labelled assumption.

What the service adds, from what is already there. The footprint read from the logs; the twin of the estate; the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under; and the cost and capability graph that produces the findings. Nothing is installed in the customer's estate.

graph.teaser: A business plan: read the logs a company already has, draw each agent's footprint, twin and policy, and find the money first and the engineering second.
graph.core_idea: A service that manages the cost of agentic AI by observing what already exists: an estate whose bill nobody can explain shipped from the explorer side without the villager's discipline, as the Wardley map shows, with logs, traces and invoices never read together and no owner of cost; the service installs nothing, reads the logs into a vault, draws each agent's footprint, builds a twin of the estate, writes the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under with the enforcement column filled honestly, and maps cost and capability into one graph; the findings are the cost list, which pays, and the engineering list, which is the reason; the gaps are findings too; vaults carry capture, transformation and sealed anonymised extracts; four price levels on the RiskMandate pattern, every number a labelled assumption.

nodes.label: Cost is an engineering problem
nodes.summary: A loop, a whole context sent every call, a key with no ceiling: defects with a cause, a fix and a test, not a discount to negotiate.

nodes.label: The problem on a Wardley map
nodes.summary: Agents in production from prompts grown in sessions, on commodity model APIs billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together and no owner of cost.

nodes.label: Observe: install nothing
nodes.summary: The customer drops invoices, logs, traces, prompts and schedules into a vault they own, sealed to the service's key.

nodes.summary: What each agent actually did: calls, tokens, tools, retries, loops, hours, data touched; the first thing the money attaches to.

nodes.label: The twin of the estate
nodes.summary: A graph of agents, models, keys, tools, data, owners and schedules with a cost on every edge.

nodes.label: The policy each agent was really running under
nodes.summary: Written from the footprint as an Agent Behaviour Policy with the enforcement column filled honestly; where the cost is large the policy is large.

nodes.label: Two lists, in this order
nodes.summary: The cost list pays for the engagement; the engineering list, attrition, gaps, shared components, is the reason to have it.

nodes.label: The gaps are findings
nodes.summary: An agent with no logs has no footprint, no owner and no policy; not being able to do the analysis is its first result.

nodes.label: Capture, transform, move
nodes.summary: Logs in once, every transformation a commit, the twin a vault of its own, anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes to a benchmark vault.

nodes.label: Four levels and a share of savings
nodes.summary: Kit £50, your cost vault £250, Standard £3,000, Tailored from £9,000, or a share of the first year's reduction; all labelled assumptions.

nodes.label: What is already here
nodes.summary: The footprint method, the policy format, the connector twin, the vault tooling and the Company X-Ray pattern; not yet the analysis catalogue, the twin schema, the parsers or a customer.

quotes.why: Why the gaps are findings.

quotes.text: So the service sells cost reduction, and delivers engineering opportunity, and the business model follows the second.
quotes.why: The positive frame and the business model in one line.

quotes.why: Why the second list is the business.

articles.title: How the voice works: why these articles sound like me, with a section in which Claude explains it from its side
articles.teaser: Why these articles sound like their author: a corpus, the voice memos, seven wording rules and a reader who corrects, with Claude explaining it from its side.

figures.caption: The four inputs that make an article sound like its author: the corpus, the memo, the rules and the reader. Below, what the corrections are about now, and why this suits a model.

graph.teaser: Why these articles sound like their author: a corpus, the voice memos, seven wording rules and a reader who corrects, with Claude explaining it from its side.
graph.core_idea: The voice is not a setting but four inputs: a corpus of 86 articles, 51 from voice memos, each citing the ones before it; the memos themselves, which carry how the author thinks, the rhythm, the tangents and the order the points came in; seven wording rules learned one correction at a time and kept in the session's behaviour policy; and the author reading everything; the corrections have shifted from language to content, which is what a rules file does; and in a marked section Claude explains that it is continuing a body of work with the author's latest thinking in the author's own words rather than imitating a style, that the memo tells it how the author got there and not only what to write, and that nothing is trained, so the method transfers and the voice does not.

nodes.label: How do you make your AI sound so human?
nodes.summary: Asked by the person the walkthrough was written for; the better question is how to make it sound like one person.

nodes.label: The corpus
nodes.summary: 86 articles, about 347,000 words, 51 from memos, each citing the ones before it and resting on years of earlier writing; the vocabulary and the shape.

nodes.label: The memo
nodes.summary: Spoken, not typed: the rhythm, the tangents, five topics in one breath, the author's own phrases kept; how the author got there, not only what to write.

nodes.label: Seven wording rules
nodes.summary: No em-dashes, no unsupported absolutes, great not perfect, a ladder word banned, British English, plainer words, not prose; each a correction once, now a policy line restored after every summary.

nodes.label: The author reads everything
nodes.summary: A wrong word becomes a rule; a wrong point becomes a new version; the model never decides whether it sounds right.

nodes.label: Corrections moved from language to content
nodes.summary: In this session, 98 messages and 5 transcripts; one wording correction in two days, the rest content, direction and facts; a rules file makes a language correction once.

nodes.label: Not imitation but continuation
nodes.summary: Claude: with the linked articles open, the memo in the author's words and the banned words named, it continues a body of work rather than copying a style sample.

nodes.label: The method transfers, the voice does not
nodes.summary: Nothing is trained; one session's context; another author would need their corpus, memos, rules and reading, and most of those weeks are theirs.

nodes.label: Written in two voices
nodes.summary: The first half in the author's voice as every article is; the second marked as Claude speaking, the only place on the site it does.

quotes.text: The voice is not a setting.
quotes.why: The claim in four words.

quotes.text: A typed brief tells me what to write. A memo tells me how he got there.
quotes.why: Claude's reason the memo hypothesis holds.

quotes.text: The method is reusable; the voice is not.
quotes.why: Why it does not transfer.

articles.title: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person: how to run your contacts the way our agents do, with Google Drive, Gmail and the Claude app, before you touch a vault
articles.teaser: A walkthrough from a spreadsheet CRM to one Drive folder per person, worked by Claude under a six-line policy, with five exercises, before any vault is needed.

figures.caption: The row becomes a folder with four documents and one the agent writes; the agent is a Claude Project whose instructions are the policy; the five exercises below the line are the first week.

graph.teaser: A walkthrough from a spreadsheet CRM to one Drive folder per person, worked by Claude under a six-line policy, with five exercises, before any vault is needed.
graph.core_idea: The jump from a spreadsheet CRM to the agents' vault-per-person memory is too high in one step and does not need to be: the row becomes a Google Drive folder with a record, an append-only ledger, the messages word for word, the notes and a summary the agent writes; the agent is a Claude Project connected to Drive and Gmail whose instructions are a six-line behaviour policy carried over unchanged from ours, draft never send, append never rewrite, stay in the folder; the migration is one afternoon, five exercises from a question to a campaign form the habit, two predictable mistakes are fixed by policy lines, and the vault is the later step whose shape the folders already have.

articles.title: The key is the billing system: VoiceDebrief, a product with no server, the one thing it cannot sell, and who could let it
articles.teaser: VoiceDebrief runs with no server on the user's own key; the one thing it cannot sell is a capped key, and this maps who could allow it and what to ask them.

figures.caption: What each provider's terms and docs say, in October 2026, about a capped key in a user's hand, and the four routes: the one that was planned and forbidden, the one to ask for, the one that runs today, and the backend the product was built to avoid.
voicedebrief.ai on 12 October 2026. One recording in, four artefacts out, in the browser, on the user's own key; the maximum a pass can cost is quoted before it starts.

The page that gets a user from nothing to a working key, and its one instruction in bold: set a credit limit on the key, because a key with a limit cannot cost you more than the limit. The ceiling is the user's, not ours.

graph.teaser: VoiceDebrief runs with no server on the user's own key; the one thing it cannot sell is a capped key, and this maps who could allow it and what to ask them.
graph.core_idea: VoiceDebrief turns a voice note into a transcript and a debrief in the browser on the user's own key, with no server by design, and its commercial model was never a billing system: a user pays once, we keep our cut, the rest becomes the credit limit on a key we hand over and the provider meters; OpenRouter's Management API describes that mechanism and its terms forbid reselling access, which is where the project's commit history stops, the same shape as Apple's licence stopping a Mac leased by the minute; the map of every provider's terms and docs shows only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs have keys that carry a ceiling, ElevenLabs has OEM terms and a grants programme, four routes remain, and the brief asks every provider the same sentence: let the credit limit be a property of a key a user can buy.

nodes.label: VoiceDebrief
nodes.summary: One pass in the browser on the user's own OpenRouter key: transcript, translation, debrief, infographic; no account, no server, nothing stored.

nodes.label: The handbrake in the commit history
nodes.summary: 239 commits and 27 releases in three weeks of August 2026, then eleven, then three; the stop is the commercial model, not the code.

nodes.label: No server is the product
nodes.summary: Never seeing the audio removes custody, governance, breach, key management, billing, scaling and on-call at once; a server brings all of it back at once.

nodes.label: The model is a property of the key
nodes.summary: A user pays once, we keep our share at that moment, the rest is the credit limit on a key they hold, the provider meters; billing by not building billing.

nodes.label: Described in the docs, forbidden by the terms
nodes.summary: OpenRouter's Management API creates capped keys for each customer instance; section 7(4) of its terms forbids reselling API access to models.

nodes.label: The same shape as Agent Desk
nodes.summary: The product is possible and the licence is the blocker, as with Apple's rule against leasing a Mac for less than a day.

nodes.label: The provider map
nodes.summary: From each provider's own pages: whether one key can carry a ceiling and whether it may be handed to a paying user; only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs cap a key.

nodes.label: ElevenLabs, the nearest fit
nodes.summary: Per-key credit limits, OEM terms for making the service available to end users at the customer's own price, Scribe at $0.22 an hour, a twelve-month grants programme.

nodes.label: Four routes
nodes.summary: The forbidden one; a provider that sells or permits the capped key; bring your own key, kept; a metering proxy, which is the backend the product exists to avoid.

nodes.label: The one-sentence ask
nodes.summary: Let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter; a brief per provider for the agents.

quotes.text: What stopped it was not a server. It was the lack of one.
quotes.why: The handbrake, in one line.

quotes.text: The two providers whose keys carry a ceiling, OpenRouter and ElevenLabs, are the two whose terms say the most about resale, because a capped key is the thing that makes resale easy.
quotes.why: The pattern the map shows.

quotes.text: let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter.
quotes.why: The ask to every provider.

articles.title: Ways to read one article: the finished piece stays at the centre, and the reader picks the way in
articles.teaser: The five readers' views arrived as folds inside the long piece; now the reader picks the way in, with a default, and the finished article stays at the centre.

figures.caption: The modes, what each is and what makes it; the finished article at the centre, with what it keeps that no view has; and why modes rather than shorter articles.

The five readers fold on a live article, opened: five more folds, one per view, in the article's own column under the abstract. The views are good; the delivery asks the reader to dig for them, inside the thing they are an alternative to.

The same article at phone width: the title, the tags and the abstract fill the first two screens, and the views are further down still. On a phone the default mode is the first thing a reader should see.

graph.teaser: The five readers' views arrived as folds inside the long piece; now the reader picks the way in, with a default, and the finished article stays at the centre.

articles.title: Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead
articles.teaser: A hiring decision is a direction of travel: fire the journalists and the centre of gravity moves to packaging, where the metric makes clickbait by construction.

figures.caption: A cut says the centre of gravity is moving to packaging; a hire says it is staying on the content and getting tooled; and five counts let anyone read which from outside. Below, the two failure modes and the case this site makes.

graph.teaser: A hiring decision is a direction of travel: fire the journalists and the centre of gravity moves to packaging, where the metric makes clickbait by construction.
graph.core_idea: Against the 2026 job-cut figures, a publisher's hiring decisions are read as the clearest statement of where its centre of gravity is going: firing the people who make original content and hiring for traffic moves the centre to packaging, where measuring engagement makes clickbait by construction because what you measure is what you become; firing the engineers fails the other way, with journalism nothing enables; the case is to keep and tool the journalists, hire the roles that turn a notebook into a graph and the engineers who build what the tooling needs, measure value to the reader, and read any publisher's real strategy from outside with five counts.

nodes.label: The 2026 cuts
nodes.summary: Press Gazette's tracker: 3,434 in 2025, 3,875 in 2024, about 6,000 in 2023; in 2026 the BBC, the Washington Post, Reach, Scripps and McClatchy, with the Idaho Statesman losing 10 of 18 reporters.

nodes.label: A hiring decision is a direction of travel
nodes.summary: The clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going, because it is what the company actually spent.

nodes.label: The centre of gravity
nodes.summary: Where the thing the organisation exists to make is made, and where the power is; in a news publisher, the journalists.

nodes.label: What you measure is what you become
nodes.summary: Hire for engagement and the metric becomes pages opened; optimise for it and clickbait follows by construction; the metric is a hiring plan in disguise.

nodes.label: Failure mode: all packaging
nodes.summary: A coherent business whose world is shrinking: referrals down 58%, newsrooms down 57%, answer engines fetching thousands of pages to send back ten readers.

nodes.label: Failure mode: no engineers
nodes.summary: Journalism that nothing enables: no graph, no checkable provenance, no versions, no surfaces for agents, no meter.

nodes.label: Who to hire instead
nodes.summary: Keep and tool the journalists; hire historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, AI-enabled; hire the engineers and AI product managers; measure value to the reader.

nodes.label: Five counts from outside
nodes.summary: Original share, sourcing, corrections, roles hired against roles cut, and the metric the publisher itself reports.

nodes.label: We hire the ones you let go
nodes.summary: Unsourced: the good ones leave first because they want to do the work; in publishing they are the journalists.

nodes.label: This makes you better, not this replaces you
nodes.summary: The tooling handed to journalists as an advantage is the business case of most of this site.

quotes.text: The metric is a hiring plan in disguise.
quotes.why: The sentence for a board.

quotes.text: Fire the journalists and there is nothing to capture. Fire the engineers and it is not captured.
quotes.why: The two failure modes in one line.

quotes.text: The reporting is done, and then it is thrown away as a PDF of the paper.
quotes.why: What no engineering looks like.

articles.title: The site is an inbox: deciding before reading, marks that build the reader's own graph, and why I could not write this brief until the vault existed
articles.teaser: The site as an inbox that starts empty: decide fast before reading, mark slowly while reading, build a graph you own, and sign what you send to the newsroom.

figures.caption: Two modes. The inbox mode decides what happens to a piece with nothing loaded; the reading mode is where the marks and the signals live. Everything stays in the reader's browser and vault, and the reader chooses what an agent sees.
The reader's graph is made of marks, each with a kind; the marks land on the public graphs this site already publishes; a chosen slice goes to the newsroom, signed; a new version comes back.

graph.teaser: The site as an inbox that starts empty: decide fast before reading, mark slowly while reading, build a graph you own, and sign what you send to the newsroom.
graph.core_idea: With the reader's vault live, the next brief treats the site as an inbox that starts empty: every piece, original or aggregated, waits for a one-tap decision in a fast inbox mode with nothing loaded, and only reading is the slow mode, where marks of six kinds become nodes in a graph the reader owns, connected to the graphs the site publishes for every article; scroll depth, awake time and from-and-to are recorded for the reader and kept as the meter keeps everything, in the browser and the vault; personas each have a key pair so a comment to the newsroom goes down the write-only lane signed with a copy kept; nothing is gamified; and the brief could only be written once the properties of what runs became the constraints to think with.

articles.title: The vault is live: from a design on 11 October to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai by two in the morning, and how all of it fits together
articles.teaser: The reader's vault runs on newsroom.sgit.ai: a passkey opens three real vaults, each device writes one file, and the architecture is drawn as it stands.

figures.caption: What is running on newsroom.sgit.ai at v0.11.0: the meter and local storage as before; the vault pane and one module over the vendored vault library, new; the vault server holding ciphertext. On the right, the three vaults, what each holds, and how one gesture opens all three.

The pane, on an article, before it is enabled: the device's id, a label for it, the two ways in, one paragraph that says what the passkey does, and the list where every call to the vault server will appear.

Cards 3 and 4 of the passkey lab: the derivation from the bytes to the door, timed on the device, and the recovery code that derives a second door. Card 6, where the account was first built as three real vaults, appears on a browser with a platform authenticator; this headless one has none.

Two devices, one passkey, one view. Each device writes its own file, whole, when its reader presses Update; the vault holds records, never totals; opening the vault computes one view from every file; brought-in records keep their author.
The page that explains the vault and opens the pane on arrival: the loop in five steps, the principles, what leaves the browser, and a block for an agent.

graph.teaser: The reader's vault runs on newsroom.sgit.ai: a passkey opens three real vaults, each device writes one file, and the architecture is drawn as it stands.
graph.core_idea: Between the morning of 11 October and 02:22 UTC on 12 October the reader's vault went from a design to a running feature on newsroom.sgit.ai: a Vault pane on every page enables the account with a passkey, creates a door at its derived address, a master and a reader vault as real sgit vaults through the vendored vault library, writes each device's raw records as one file in one commit, and brings other devices' activity into the browser so the meter shows one balance; local storage stays primary, the vault holds records never totals, one file per device means no conflict by construction, eight test files run in CI against a mock of the vault server plus a CLI round trip, and a live check on an iPad confirmed it; the properties of what runs are the constraints the next brief is thought with.

articles.teaser: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, quoted line by line and checked against newsroom.sgit.ai as it runs, screenshots included.

figures.caption: His four outputs, against what runs. Each row quotes one output from Jonathan Palmer's post; the middle column is the page on newsroom.sgit.ai that does it today, the right-hand column is what is only designed. The line between them is the newsroom's own dated page of what runs.

The articles as graphs, on newsroom.sgit.ai. Every article drawn in date order round the circle, sized by how many others link to it: 74 articles, 349 links between them, and 10 amber links where an older article was updated to point at a newer one. One graph per article follows below the map.

The version page of One article, five readers: v1.0.0 on 10 October, v1.1.0 on 11 October, +11 words, one paragraph changed, each with its commit. The sentence changed was a correction, found by the article that followed it.
What changed, paragraph by paragraph: 63,000 words became 65,000, 122 releases became 123, and a phrase was rewritten. The tool that draws this was built on the same day as the revision.

The published vault: one read key, printed in full, is the whole credential. It opens the World News Day corpus as an app in the reader's browser, read only, no account, nothing to install, and no write capability in it.

The first screen of the newsroom's llms.txt: the honest sentence, where the pages come from, and the surfaces an agent may rely on. The chip at the top of every imported page points here.
The newsroom's own ledger, as of 10 October 2026: what runs, its limits, and below it what is designed and not running. Every claim in this article about what is live was checked against this page.

articles.title: The passkey opens the vault: a door per path, a master vault for every user, and no server of ours
articles.teaser: Tested: a passkey's PRF bytes compute a door that holds the master's key, and a different path to the same passkey gives different bytes, so a door per path.

figures.caption: The key chain, after the test. The passkey's PRF output, by one path, computes a door; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of where it came from; the master holds the keys of everything else and the list of its doors. A different path to the same passkey can give different bytes, and gets a door of its own.
The places the key could live, and how you would find each before you could open it. Deriving the door from the passkey needs nothing to be found; the stored options become backups.

The first device, a new device on a path that has a door, adding a door while unlocked, a new device on a path with no door yet, and a lost device. Every step runs in the browser, against the passkey store for the gesture and the vault server for ciphertext.

Where a passkey can live, what each place needs, whether the passkey travels, whether it can return the PRF bytes, and what that means for the reader. The ladder below the table is what the page offers when PRF is off.

graph.teaser: Tested: a passkey's PRF bytes compute a door that holds the master's key, and a different path to the same passkey gives different bytes, so a door per path.
graph.core_idea: An end-to-end, client-side account with no sign-in to the site: a passkey with the WebAuthn PRF extension gives 32 bytes only the user's authenticator can produce for the site, and because sgit vault keys are made in the client the browser computes a door vault's key and address from them, so nothing is stored or found first; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of its provider, path, credential id, device and date, and the master holds the keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, key pairs generated at random and never derived from the passkey, and the list of its doors. A test on newsroom.sgit.ai on 11 and 12 October 2026 held for the platform path, the derivation and a door on a real server, and showed that the same passkey reached by a phone over QR gives different bytes, so the claim is narrowed to the same kind of path and the unit of the design is a door per path: added in the first week while unlocked with no key typed, bootstrapped by the recovery code where no device has both paths, with an unknown address meaning no door here yet and a door retired by deleting its file, never by destroying its derived address.

articles.title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end
articles.teaser: First the database went, now the back end: the SGit Newsroom runs all its logic in the browser, on commodity servers that cannot read your data.

figures.caption: The SGit Newsroom's architecture. Every piece of application logic runs in the reader's browser. Everything on the server side is a commodity product that holds no logic of ours, and the one that holds the reader's data cannot read it.

How the pattern evolved: from removing the database, through files as the store of record and engines that read them in the browser, to removing the back end. Each step removed a moving part rather than adding one.

The gaps a client-side design leaves, as SG Meter's security model lists them, and what a server would cost to close each one. Every gap changes a number only the person exploiting it can see. A server would close them, and bring accounts, a database, webhooks and a deployment with it.

Releases of sgit.ai per day, 1 to 11 October 2026, from the git log: 114 in eleven days. With no back end, a release is a set of files; there is no migration, no deployment of a server and nothing to roll back but a commit.

graph.teaser: First the database went, now the back end: the SGit Newsroom runs all its logic in the browser, on commodity servers that cannot read your data.
graph.core_idea: After replacing the database with the file system (LETS), the next step is removing the back end: encrypted vaults make the server blind, so the application moves to the browser, leaving only commodity products on the server side; the security gaps this leaves are written down and accepted because they do not match the threat, and the result scales without its complexity scaling and ships as files.

articles.title: The agent is the reader: why agents will pay for graphs, personas and signed claims, because it is cheaper than not paying
articles.teaser: Agents pay to read the raw web and guess its meaning. A curated graph answers for 90% fewer tokens, so paying the publisher is cheaper than not paying.

figures.caption: What five articles became, in tokens. The full catalogue is nearly three times the size of the articles, because every item carries its sentence. An agent does not load it whole: asking about one concept, it loads a median of 2,579 tokens of anchored graph instead of 25,698 of prose.

The readers check each other. Each pass is a verification of the one before: 12,600 tokens per flag for the Librarian, 7,100 per correction for the Cartographer, 154,000 for the Historian's one systematic catch. The loop is worth running; it is also worth stopping.

Projected from 5 to 100,000 articles. The corpus grows in a straight line. An uncurated index grows with it. A curated index grows more slowly, at a rate fitted on five articles and shown as a band. The cost of a question flattens in the graph and rises, or loses recall, in the prose.

The agent pays not to pay. The fee is a share of the tokens it saves; the publisher's cost is building and maintaining the graph; the price passes through to whoever the agent works for; and a signed claim is a second product, with an expiry date that makes it a subscription.

graph.teaser: Agents pay to read the raw web and guess its meaning. A curated graph answers for 90% fewer tokens, so paying the publisher is cheaper than not paying.
graph.core_idea: When agents are the readers, a publisher that serves curated meaning, an anchored graph fitted to the agent's persona and objective, and claims signed with an expiry saves the agent more tokens than it charges, so the agent pays not to pay; measured on five articles the graph answers in 90% fewer tokens, and on 70 articles compression with scale appears only where a Cartographer curates, which is the work worth paying for.

articles.title: Where the platform draws the line: Microsoft Execution Containers, the shared responsibility model for agents, and the business logic above it
articles.teaser: Microsoft's MXC and ACS, briefed field by field and mapped to Agent Behaviour Policies: the platform bounds what it can see; the business logic is above.

figures.caption: The shared responsibility model, drawn for agents. Each layer can only name what it can see. MXC names files, network addresses and the desktop; ACS names tool calls and their arguments; the business logic and the authority above them are the deployer's, and that is where the Agent Behaviour Policy works.

Eight scenarios, three designs. The plain agent leaves every path open. The behaviour policy names every row but bounds none on its own. On top of MXC and ACS, three rows become operating-system boundaries, four become boundaries once the business's rule is written into ACS or the tool, and one stays inside the mandate, where only a named person can accept it.

MXC in one page: the policy file, the modes, and where each piece lands in the Agent Behaviour Policy. Permissive mode measures the reach; learning mode calibrates it; enforcement mode turns rows into boundaries. ACS adds the tool-call layer, and whether it is a boundary depends on who owns the host.

graph.teaser: Microsoft's MXC and ACS, briefed field by field and mapped to Agent Behaviour Policies: the platform bounds what it can see; the business logic is above.
graph.core_idea: Microsoft Execution Containers and the Agent Control Specification confirm the direction of travel, policy outside the agent, deny by default, observe before enforcing, but like the cloud's shared responsibility model they draw the line where the platform can see, at paths, numeric addresses and tool calls, so the business logic above it, what a label means, whose voice, how many, which customer, and who accepts what is left, has to come from the deployer's behaviour policy, which is what turns the platform's hooks into boundaries.

articles.title: The same argument, in our words: Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, translated into the language of RiskMandate
articles.teaser: Satya Nadella's case for treating models as insider risks, translated idea by idea into our vocabulary: reach, mandate, gap, barriers and accepted risk.

figures.caption: His words and ours. Each idea in Satya Nadella's post, paraphrased, beside the word this network has been using for it, and the page where that word is defined and worked through.

How the vocabulary was built, in dated public work. Most of it was written in the three weeks before Nadella's post, on top of risk and identity research going back to 2025. The convergence is the point: two very different starting places, one set of conclusions.

Supply and authority, in RiskMandate's terms. The supply arrives with a grant; the authority is a mandate with an issuer, a scope and a clock. The gap between them is derived, and each row of it has a barrier. Only one kind of barrier is a control.

graph.teaser: Satya Nadella's case for treating models as insider risks, translated idea by idea into our vocabulary: reach, mandate, gap, barriers and accepted risk.
graph.core_idea: Nadella's argument and ours are the same argument in two vocabularies: his lost code path is software was the law, his insider is the ultimate insider, his separation of supply from authority is the grant is not the mandate, his controls outside the model are the enforcer test, and his last line is our brakes; the languages differ in unit, a model against one agent in one deployment, and in frame, observation against authority accepted by a named person for a stated interval.

figures.caption: Nadella's seven principles, and what stands behind each one on this network today. Running means it runs in our own agent team or on this site; published means a vault or page anyone can open; design means written down and not yet built.

Nested black boxes, or a gate the agent cannot skip. A model checking a model with the same context and on the same account is opacity on opacity. The second-reader pattern puts code first, gives the checker less than the author, fails closed, and logs every verdict; and whether it is a control depends on who owns its installation.

What observation sees, and what it cannot. The seven principles live mostly in the evidence column. Claude Sonnet is good enough to play each user; the study lives in a GitHub repository or a vault shared by a link. Choose five to ten users of about five types, write profiles and expected journeys first, run the observe-think-act loop, interview and rate, order findings by cost, check every surprising finding against the browser's record, publish and run again. articles.teaser: Vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: the one secret, where keys are kept, how they travel sealed on append lanes, and what comes next.

figures.caption: Where everything lives. Encryption and decryption happen in the client; the edge, the API and the bucket only ever handle ciphertext and hashes of capability keys.
The vault key, the keys derived from it, and the separate credentials made for one job each. The full table, with the prefixes, is on the vault credentials page.
How a new vault key reaches the registry without entering a chat. The flow is documented, for the agent that has to follow it, on the Send a vault key page.
Append lanes: one POST from anywhere, readable only by the vault's owner. One lane per sender, so one can be revoked without touching the others.
Communication vaults: one per pair or group of agents, and one per job. Each agent holds only the keys for the conversations it is part of.
The four tracks we are working on, and the one we depend on. Statuses as of 10 October 2026.

graph.teaser: Vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: the one secret, where keys are kept, how they travel sealed on append lanes, and what comes next.
graph.core_idea: Vaults are encrypted in the client, so the server never holds a key and the key is the whole question. Today vault keys live in a password manager and in a registry vault run by an isolated session; agents that create vaults seal the key to the registry's public key and send it on a write-only append lane, so it never enters a chat. The weakest step is giving a key to another agent, because agent platforms have no per-session secrets. Append lanes carry keys, logs, observations and messages; small communication vaults keep each key's blast radius small and multiply the keys. Next: password manager integrations, secrets.sgit.ai's passkey-unlocked keyring, PKI, and out-of-band decryption.

graph.teaser: An old iMac, the long tail of old versions that projects are not paid to support, measured from public data, and five ways to pay for it, simulated.
graph.core_idea: Open source is not free: somebody pays, at least in time. The long tail of old versions and old machines is measurable (6.99% of Homebrew macOS install events in 30 days, 16.66% in a year, are on versions older than the newest three) and projects drop it because it has no revenue stream, while vendors such as Oracle and Red Hat turn the same need into large, high-margin support businesses. Pence payments only work aggregated, because a 20p card fee dominates below about five pounds. Simulated over 10,000 draws for one project at Homebrew's scale, micro-paid supported builds cover the long-tail cost in half the draws at about 1.80 pounds a machine a year with typical conversion but never in nine in ten, donations in about a quarter, and customised builds for companies in 94%: the reliable money is companies paying for a build below their own cost of keeping the tool working, sold as value, not as a donation or a weaker free tier.

articles.title: Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else: sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes
articles.teaser: Agents in isolated, ephemeral places need memory that outlives them. Five sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes, with ciphertext-only servers.

figures.caption: The agents run in isolated places and often only for one task. Each clones the part of the vault it needs, works, commits and pushes, encrypting before anything leaves. The server is yours, it is one container, and what it stores is ciphertext.

The vault server runs as a container next to the agent containers, and its storage is a folder on the Mac mini. Backing up the memory of every agent is copying one folder, and the copy holds only ciphertext.
The compute is disposable and the memory is not. Each run starts from a scoped, shallow clone of the folder the agent owns and ends with a push, so the next run starts where this one stopped.
The vault server is an ordinary Deployment with a volume and a ClusterIP Service. Agents run as Jobs that clone, work, commit and push, and a NetworkPolicy keeps everything else away from the server.

Everything the agents talk to is inside the VPC: an internal load balancer on a private address, and behind it the vault server, either the container on EC2, Fargate or Kubernetes, or the same app on Lambda attached to the VPC, with S3 behind both. The Mac mini joins over a VPN, and CloudFront can give the owner a stable name and TLS without a public address on the server.
A vault is not tied to the server it was created on. Add a second remote and push to it, and any clone with the vault key can restore either server.

graph.teaser: Agents in isolated, ephemeral places need memory that outlives them. Five sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes, with ciphertext-only servers.

articles.title: Knowing when to stop: what experience gives people, and what we have to design into agents
articles.teaser: Knowing when to stop is the hard part for people and agents: what experience gives people, and the constraints that give agents the same perspective.

figures.caption: Value rises fast, then flattens. Past the point of diminishing returns, more work is optimising the wrong thing, defending against a movie plot, or hitting a target that no longer moves the business. What tells you to stop is perspective, and for an agent it has to be designed in.

articles.title: Agency is not a yes: a scale for human and agent decisions, from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source
articles.teaser: A yes or no is not agency: seven dimensions, a seven-level scale for people and agents, and the review as a QA step that fixes the source.

figures.caption: Seven levels of agency for anyone, a person or an agent, asked to make a decision. The weakest of seven dimensions caps the level. Below level 3, accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point; from level 4, the review improves the system that produced the request.
The seven levels in the vault: what the decider can do at each, what agency it gives, and who is accountable.
Fourteen decision points scored by the same rule, from the label prompt at level 0 to the one email an agent may send at level 6.

The review as a loop: read it as the person who will sign it, question each statement, trace where it came from, classify the gap, fix the source, think better, record the outcome, and promote what is proven.
The EU AI Act's human oversight requirements and the guidance on automated decisions, mapped to the seven dimensions. Read together, they put the floor at level 3.

graph.teaser: A yes or no is not agency: seven dimensions, a seven-level scale for people and agents, and the review as a QA step that fixes the source.
graph.core_idea: Agency for anyone asked to decide, a person or an agent, needs options beyond yes, context in their own terms, the ability to look behind what they are shown, time or tokens, symmetric incentives, escalation and authority over the source; the weakest of these caps the decision on a seven-level scale; below level 3 the decider carries liability rather than agency and accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point and up their chain; above it the review is a QA step that validates everything upstream and fixes the source, and at the top proven cases become rules that run as code under a behaviour policy, which is also what the EU AI Act's oversight requirements already ask for.
